To limp means to walk in an uneven, labored way because one leg or foot is hurt, weak, or painful. When you limp, you cannot put your full weight on one leg, so each step you take is asymmetrical — one side dips, drags, or moves differently from the other, giving your walk a lopsided, struggling quality.

A normal walk has a steady, even rhythm. A limp breaks that rhythm. One step feels normal; the next is shorter, slower, or guarded. The body instinctively tries to protect the painful leg by shifting as much work as possible to the healthy one.

"After twisting his ankle on the stairs, he limped to the sofa and sat down."

"She limped off the football field, clutching her knee."

Anything that makes bearing weight on one leg painful or difficult can cause a limp:

  • A sprained or broken ankle
  • A blister or cut on the foot
  • Knee or hip pain
  • Muscle soreness after intense exercise
  • A long-term condition like arthritis

The key idea is pain or weakness in one leg that makes walking normally impossible.

The word applies equally to animals.

"The dog had stepped on a thorn and was limping badly."

"The horse limped back to the stable after the race."

This is where the word becomes especially interesting and widely used. "Limp" is frequently used to describe anything — not just a person or animal — that moves forward slowly and with great difficulty, usually because it is damaged or barely functional.

Vehicles and machines:

"The damaged ship limped back to port on one engine."

"After the crash, the car limped to the nearest garage."

Here, the ship and car are obviously not in physical pain, but they are moving the way an injured person would — struggling, barely managing, not at full capacity.

Organizations, economies, projects:

"The company limped through the financial crisis, losing staff and customers every month."

"After the scandal, the campaign limped along with almost no funding."

In these cases, "limp" conveys that something is surviving, but only just — it is not thriving, not moving at full speed, not in good health. It carries a sense of strain, struggle, and fragility.

A very common phrase you will hear is "limp to the finish line", which means to barely complete something after a long, difficult, exhausting struggle — arriving at the end, but in a weakened state.

"The project limped to the finish line, three months late and over budget."

"Limp" is often paired with small directional words that sharpen its meaning:

  • Limp along — to continue moving or functioning, but with difficulty and without real progress. "The peace talks limped along for months with no agreement."
  • Limp away / limp off — to leave a place while limping. "He was hit by a ball and limped away from the pitch."
  • Limp back — to return somewhere while limping, often implying defeat or damage. "The soldiers limped back to camp after the failed mission."
  • Limp home — to reach home or safety, but in a damaged or exhausted state. "The battered ship finally limped home after weeks at sea."

Several words describe difficult walking, but each has its own flavor.

Hobble — like limp, but more extreme. A person who hobbles takes very small, stiff steps and looks as though every step is painful. It suggests more severe difficulty than a limp. You might also use a stick or crutch when you hobble. A limp can be mild; a hobble rarely is.

Shuffle — to drag your feet along the ground, barely lifting them. A shuffle is not necessarily caused by injury — tired people shuffle, elderly people sometimes shuffle. A limp involves uneven steps; a shuffle involves slow, dragging steps on both feet.

Stagger — to move unsteadily, nearly falling, swaying from side to side. Staggering is caused by loss of balance (dizziness, exhaustion, or intoxication), not necessarily injury. It looks more chaotic than a limp.

Trudge — to walk slowly and heavily due to tiredness or effort, but without injury. A trudge is even and labored; a limp is uneven and protective.

Of all these, limp is the most specific about the cause: one leg is compromised, and the body is compensating for it.

"Limp" carries a tone of vulnerability and effort. When you say someone limped somewhere, you automatically create a picture of a person who has been hurt but is still pushing forward. There is something quietly determined about a limp — the person is not stopping, but they are clearly struggling. This emotional weight is why the figurative uses work so well: a company that "limps along" isn't giving up, but it is clearly in trouble.

At its simplestTo walk unevenly because one leg hurts or is weak
FigurativelyTo move, function, or progress slowly and with great difficulty, usually due to damage
The core feelingStruggle, effort, barely managing, pushing through pain or hardship
